text.p: Speedy Swede Glenn Magnusson spoilt Mario Cipollini's Giro d'Italia dream on Friday.
His finishing burst took him a second clear of the charging pack with Cipollini third behind another Italian, Mirko Rossato, at the end of the 150-km race from Varazze.
Cipollini was hunting a personal record of five wins in a Giro, but Magnusson said: "Once I was ahead in the final 500 metres I knew I could win.
"It is good to beat Cipollini but he is not the real Cipollini because his team has been weakened. I knew I might have a chance today because I beat him in an intermediate sprint on Thursday."
The big Tuscan knew he was beaten. "When Sergei Outschakov crashed most of us had to brake quickly, but Magnusson was the lucky guy who was not affected by it."
As Outschakov led the strung-out pack into a corner his wheels slid away, dumping him at the feet of spectators, but he was able to ride to the finish.
An unruffled Pavel Tonkov, wearing his leader's pink jersey for a 10th day, and his chief threat, Frenchman Luc Leblanc, finished 11th and 12th in the mass finish.
The Russian is ready for Saturday's test which finishes on the 2,008m Breuil Cervinia, the third mountain climb of the 232-km stage which takes the race close to the Swiss border.
"My rivals have to show that they can beat me. Ivan Gotti says it will be the most important day, but he has to prove that he is stronger than me in Wednesday's time trial," Tonkov said.
"I have to give my adversaries a sense of security to show them that I am sure of myself, but expect a big battle.
"I have learnt in this Giro when to control the race and when to attack. I may even try on Saturday."
Gotti has a deficit of 1:07 and is third overall. He was fifth last year, but with Marco Pantani and Enrico Zaina out of the Giro, he is now the only real hope for Italy.
Pantani crashed out a week ago, and Zaina, second last year, pulled out before Friday's start with prostate problems.
